message.content:
Below is a concise summary of key tenant‑rights protections under Texas law (Texas Property Code). This is general information and **not** legal advice; if you have a specific dispute, consult a licensed attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization. | Area | What the law says | Practical take‑away | |------|-------------------|---------------------| | **Security Deposit** | Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for residential units (or two months for furnished units) and must return it within 30 days after lease ends, minus deductions for damages beyond normal wear & tear. | Keep records of the unit’s condition at move‑in/move‑out (photos, written inventory). | | **Habitability / Repairs** | Landlord must keep premises safe, sanitary, and fit for habitation (Sections 24.001–24.005). Failure to maintain basic utilities or structural integrity can be grounds for withholding rent or terminating the lease. | Document problems promptly (written notice + photos). If landlord doesn’t fix issues, you may withhold rent *only* after following proper procedure (see below). | | **Rent Payment & Withholding** | You may withhold rent only if the landlord has failed to repair serious defects after being notified in writing. The withheld amount must equal the actual cost of repairs. | Never withhold rent without first giving written notice and allowing a reasonable time for repairs. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For non‑payment of rent: 3‑day notice to pay or vacate.
• For lease violations: 10‑day notice to cure or vacate (unless the violation is a “material” breach).
• For termination of month‑to‑month tenancy: 30‑day written notice (or 60 days if the tenant has lived there for ≥1 year). | Always serve notices in person or via certified mail and keep copies. | | **Eviction Process** | Landlord must file an unlawful detainer action in court. Court will issue a summons and order a hearing. Tenant gets a chance to respond. | Do not ignore eviction notices; respond promptly and consider hiring counsel. | | **Discrimination** | Under federal Fair Housing Act and Texas Civil Rights Code § 21.01, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or handicap. | Report discrimination to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or Texas Attorney General. | | **Right to Privacy** | Landlord must give reasonable notice (usually 24 hours) before entering the unit, except in emergencies. | Keep a log of all entries; if landlord enters without notice, you may have a claim. | | **Lease Terms** | A lease is a binding contract. Landlord cannot unilaterally change terms unless both parties agree. | Read the lease carefully; ask questions before signing. | | **Legal Resources** | • Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division (https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection)
• Texas Tenants’ Association (https://texastenants.org/)
• Local city or county housing departments | These sites offer forms, guides, and sometimes free legal clinics. | ### Quick Checklist When You Move In 1. **Get a written lease** (even if it’s a verbal agreement, try to get it in writing). 2. **Document the unit’s condition** (take dated photos, list existing damage). 3. **Keep receipts** for any repairs you pay for yourself. 4. **Know the required notice periods** for ending tenancy or responding to notices. If you’re facing a specific situation—like a landlord refusing to make repairs, receiving an eviction notice, or suspecting discrimination—contact a local tenant‑rights group or a lawyer who specializes in landlord‑tenant law. They can help you interpret how the statutes apply to your case and guide you through any legal filings.
